new_statements.quote: Kemaloh Lun Bawang stress is not contrastive and appears, from the available data, to usually fall on a word's final syllable. When a word is spoken in isolation or occurs at the end of an intonational phrase, this stress is quite pronounced, seemingly thanks to the amplifying effects of a strong boundary tone. Outside this context, the contrast between the penultimate and final syllables of a word is much less obvious, with fairly similar weight given to each and only a slight, though highly consistent, preference for the ultima. ... Though stress seems to be predominantly final, it is not uniformly so; a small number of words consistently display penultimate stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress on the final syllable (ultima); prominence difference between penult and ultima is small outside phrase-final position but consistently favours the ultima; antepenult is clearly weakest (with vowel neutralization). Author concludes (p.55) 'Lun Bawang has word-final stress', supported by acoustic measures, final-syllable clipping of names/common words, and iambic meter with ultima-only rhyme.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; only that in trisyllables+ the antepenult is 'noticeably unstressed by comparison to both the penult and the ultima'.
new_statements.exceptions: A small set of words consistently penultimate (pelanuk 'mouse-deer', buayeh 'crocodile', lematek 'leech'); kereb 'time, when' shows no consistent penult/ultima difference; ngecekuh 'because' tends to antepenultimate stress. Author flags the analysis as provisional (fieldwork cancelled; stress vs. intonation not fully disentangled) and notes Blust 2006's earlier report of near-even stress with penult preference for older Kelabit/Lun Dayeh speakers.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level claim; final stress is most salient in isolation/IP-final position (boundary tone), and the author explicitly factors out IP-final tokens and open final syllables (final vowels always long) before concluding final stress. Blust's note (quoted p.52) that N. Sarawak languages show 'final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context' is discussed and an alternative boundary-tone interpretation raised.
new_statements.identity_note: puto1237 'Putoh' [put] is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry (ISO code still Active). Ethnologue 15 defined it as the Dayic variety of the Mentarang River, N. Kalimantan (Long Berang, Mensalong, Bangalan) with dialects 'Pa Kembaloh' and 'Abai'; Glottolog now files these as Lundayeh lund1271 dialects pake1237 'Pa Kembaloh' and abai1239 'Abai' (Wikipedia treats Abai as Murutic, misassigned). 'Putuk/Putoh' is an exonym (< Seputuk River) for Dayic-speaking peoples (Mortensen 2021:19). The quoted statement describes Kemaloh Lun Bawang (= Pa' Kemaloh, i.e. pake1237), the lingua-franca dialect originating on the Kemaloh tributary of the Krayan; Mortensen (p.209) says the Long Berang (Mentarang) dialect 'does not appear to differ significantly from the Kemaloh dialect except by a couple of sound changes'. A catalog entry should be keyed to lund1271 (dialect pake1237), not to the bookkeeping code puto1237; the same file is held under kela1258 and is also the natural source for the lund1271 target.

sources.note: Sec. 3.4 (printed pp.51-56): stress not contrastive; usually word-final, strongly so in isolation/IP-final position (boundary tone), otherwise only a slight but consistent preference for the ultima over the penult; antepenult clearly unstressed; a few words (pelanuk, buayeh, lematek) consistently penultimate; ngecekuh antepenultimate. Supports final stress with acoustic measurements (Table 3.6), clipping to the final syllable, and iambic meter/ultima-only rhyme.
